macro: This is a company-specific earnings newsletter focused on Wednesday October 21 before-market-open reporters. There is no broad index or overnight macro commentary included in this edition. Risk tone and broad market context are not addressed.
rates_fed: No Fed, rates, or dollar commentary is included in this newsletter. However, M/I Homes explicitly flags higher mortgage interest rates as a key headwind depressing housing demand and margins.
market_outlook: No explicit directional market call is made. The earnings slate is mixed — healthcare and industrials are broadly constructive, financials are nuanced, housing is a clear pressure point, and AT&T's competitive overhang from SpaceX adds an uncertainty layer to telecom.
bull_case: Danaher, Thermo Fisher, Elevance, AT&T, and Wabtec all delivered beats with raised full-year guidance, suggesting underlying corporate earnings resilience. Nvidia's capacity expansion plans signal continued aggressive AI infrastructure investment. Healthcare names like Abbott and DHR show improving end-market trends that could lift the broader sector.
bear_case: Moody's missed on both EPS and revenue, Northern Trust's core fee revenue disappointed, and M/I Homes posted a large shortfall while flagging worsening housing market conditions. Abbott's Medical Devices segment fell short — the second consecutive miss from a major device firm after J&J — raising sector-level concerns. SpaceX's reiterated intent to enter the wireless market is a persistent overhang for telecom.

company_items.summary: Philip Morris beat Q3 EPS at $2.36 versus the Street's $2.30 and delivered organic growth of 7.1% versus the expected 5.4%. Despite the beat, management only reiterated full-year FX-neutral EPS guidance of $8.11–$8.26, citing geopolitical headwinds and energy-related cost inflation from the Middle East conflict pressuring Q4 input prices.

Moody's missed Q3 EPS at $4.14 versus the Street's $4.27 and revenue at $2.023 billion versus the expected $2.076 billion. The company reiterated its prior full-year guidance, offering limited incremental positive catalyst to offset the top- and bottom-line shortfall.

Northern Trust posted a large headline EPS beat at $3.40 versus the Street's $2.88, but approximately $50 million in one-time pre-tax tailwinds flattered the number. Core fee revenue missed at $1.373 billion versus the expected $1.405 billion and the Q4 revenue outlook of plus 6–7% fell short of the Street's 7.4% estimate.

Abbott reported Q3 EPS of $1.42 and revenue growth of 7% — essentially inline with consensus — and reiterated full-year guidance. Nutrition and Diagnostics outperformed while Medical Devices fell short, marking the second consecutive miss from a major device company after J&J. Abbott also announced plans to spin off its Nutrition business — home to Ensure, PediaSure, Glucerna, and Similac — into an independent public company by end of 2027.

Danaher delivered solid Q3 EPS upside at $2.11 versus the Street's $1.92 with core revenue growth of 3% at the high end of guidance and 110 basis points of adjusted operating margin expansion. Full-year EPS guidance was nudged higher to $8.57–$8.62 from the prior $8.45–$8.60, but the Q4 core revenue growth guide of 3% fell well short of the Street's 5.1% expectation.

Elevance posted a headline EPS beat of $6.99 versus the Street's $4.68, though $1.85 of that was a non-operating tailwind, leaving adjusted EPS of $5.14 — still a solid beat. The medical cost ratio came in at 90.6%, about 75 basis points better than consensus, and full-year EPS guidance was raised to at least $29 from at least $27, with the 2026 baseline lifted by 75 cents and 2027 EPS implied above $30 versus the Street at $29.60.

Thermo Fisher delivered strong Q3 upside with EPS 15% above the prior year at $6.68 versus the Street's $6.41 and organic revenue growth of 6% versus the expected 4.2%. Full-year EPS guidance was raised to $25.13–$25.43 from the prior $24.64–$25.12, a clean beat-and-raise quarter.

M/I Homes reported a large Q3 EPS miss at $2.56 versus the Street's $3.26 as higher mortgage rates weigh on demand and inflation pressures margins. Management explicitly cited increasingly difficult market conditions including weaker demand and growing economic uncertainty, painting a gloomy picture for the near-term housing outlook.

Wabtec beat Q3 EPS at $2.83 versus the Street's $2.74, driven by strong margin expansion of 190 basis points to 22.9%. Full-year EPS guidance was raised to a midpoint of $10.95 from $10.75, though revenue fell slightly short at $3.12 billion versus $3.2 billion expected and the 12-month backlog declined sequentially.

AT&T beat Q3 EPS at 65 cents versus 60 cents expected and revenue of $32.3 billion versus $31.7 billion, achieving its best service revenue growth in over four years, while EBITDA of $12.5 billion also topped estimates. Full-year EPS guidance was raised to $2.40 from the prior $2.25–$2.35 and long-term capex was nudged lower to $22–$23 billion per year. However, SpaceX management reiterated plans to be a major wireless market competitor, keeping a significant competitive overhang on the stock.

sectors: Healthcare devices are showing a pattern of weakness — both J&J and Abbott's Medical Devices segments have now missed, warranting caution on the broader med-tech group. Housing remains under acute pressure from elevated mortgage rates and margin compression, as evidenced by M/I Homes' large shortfall. Telecom faces a structural competitive threat from SpaceX entering the wireless market. Industrial and life science tools names like Wabtec and Thermo Fisher are showing resilient execution with raised guidance.
tts_summary:
Good morning. This is your earnings rundown for Wednesday October 21st, covering the before-market-open slate. There is no broad macro or Fed commentary in today's note — this is purely a company-specific earnings edition, so let's get right into it.

Starting with healthcare, which is the most active sector this morning. Thermo Fisher is the cleanest beat-and-raise of the group — EPS came in 15% above year-ago levels at $6.68 versus the Street's $6.41, organic revenue grew 6% against a 4.2% estimate, and full-year guidance was raised. That's a strong print. Elevance also beat handily — headline EPS of $6.99 versus $4.68 expected, though about $1.85 of that was a non-operating item. Strip that out and you still have a solid beat at $5.14. The medical cost ratio came in 75 basis points better than consensus, full-year guidance was raised to at least $29, and management is guiding 2027 EPS above $30. Danaher beat on EPS and margins with 110 basis points of operating margin expansion, but the Q4 revenue guide of 3% core growth missed the Street's 5.1% — so a mixed read there. Abbott was essentially inline on EPS and revenue with full-year guidance reiterated, but Medical Devices came up short — and that's now the second consecutive miss from a major device company after Johnson and Johnson, which is worth watching as a sector-level signal. Abbott also announced plans to spin off its Nutrition division into a standalone public company by end of 2027.

In financials, Moody's missed on both EPS and revenue — $4.14 versus $4.27 on earnings and $2.02 billion versus $2.08 billion on sales — with no guidance raise to offset the shortfall. Northern Trust had a big headline beat at $3.40 versus $2.88, but about $50 million in one-time pre-tax items flattered that number, core fee revenue missed, and the Q4 outlook was light.

In telecom, AT&T delivered a solid quarter — EPS of 65 cents beat the 60-cent estimate, revenue grew 5.3% to $32.3 billion, EBITDA topped estimates, and full-year EPS guidance was raised to $2.40. The issue is SpaceX. Management reiterated Tuesday night they plan to be a major player in the wireless market, and that overhang isn't going away.

In industrials, Wabtec beat on EPS and raised full-year guidance, though revenue missed slightly and the backlog declined sequentially — a modest mixed print. Winnebago was roughly inline on earnings thanks to cost controls, but revenue and gross margins missed and fiscal 2027 EPS guidance came in well below plan at $1.95 versus $2.30 expected.

In housing, M/I Homes posted a large miss — $2.56 versus $3.26 expected — and management was direct about deteriorating conditions: higher mortgage rates, weaker demand, and growing economic uncertainty. The housing sector remains under significant pressure.

Finally, Nvidia announced plans to increase substrate capacity by 2.5 times over the next three years and expects total semiconductor testing capacity to double from 2026 to 2027 — a continued signal of aggressive AI infrastructure buildout.

Bottom line: the overall earnings tape is constructive in life sciences and select industrials, mixed in financials and telecom, and clearly challenged in housing and med-tech devices. Stay disciplined and size accordingly.
